title: Continuous systems cannot exceed discrete computation in practice

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Continuous systems cannot exceed discrete computation in practice

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Continuous systems, including analog computers, systems described by continuous equations, and even idealized perfectly continuous systems under reasonable assumptions, cannot perform computations fundamentally more sophisticated than discrete systems like cellular automata; continuity is largely an idealization.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: even idealized perfectly continuous systems will never in fact be able to perform fundamentally more sophisticated computations.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 12, “The Principle of Computational Equivalence”; section “The Validity of the Principle” (from p. 726), p. 730. Scope: analog computers, continuous mathematical models, and physical systems treated as continuous

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch12-08: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.57

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Computable-analysis theorems resolve substantial model classes, and physical precision limits constrain real analog devices. The claim's inclusion of idealized continuous systems under unspecified 'reasonable assumptions' prevents a single complete test.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Specify physically reasonable continuity, noise, precision, and resource assumptions, then prove that each continuous evolution can be simulated to required observable accuracy by a Turing machine. Explicit continuous models computing nonrecursive functions under those assumptions would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The result depends critically on computable parameters, finite precision, robustness, and resource bounds.

Ideal mathematical continuity is not itself experimentally testable.

Different analog-computation models have different power.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Under the finite-encoding condition the book emphasizes, computable analysis already proves that many ordinary continuous models stay within Turing computation, and that literature is public. The claim also bundles practical analog machines and every idealized continuum, and those pieces do not share one theorem. Dropping the encoding condition is a known way to write equations that look more powerful, so the test is only as strong as the assumption.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Fix finite discrete encoding of inputs and outputs. Within that constraint, confirm the claim if analog machines, standard continuous equations, and idealized continuous models only compute Turing-computable functions; refute it by a continuous model, meeting the constraint, that decides a non-recursive set.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Historical analog computers being slower than digital computers does not by itself bound idealized continuous models.

Reasonable assumptions do the real work: exact real oracles or infinite-time supertasks can exceed Turing computation if the assumption is dropped.
